quoted_phrases: --- {   "id": "21c-ai-rewrite-belonging-superpower",   "title": "Belonging Is a Superpower (AI version)",   "author": "AI (model unspecified)",   "year": 2026,   "period": "21st",   "format": "Patterns for decentralised organising; matched-pair AI version of Oliver Sylvester-Bradley's 2017 essay",   "source_url": "rewrite",   "fetch_status": 200,   "extract_method": "manual_paste",   "human_pair": "21c-opencoop-belonging-superpower",   "expected_use": [     "genre_paired_corpus",     "human_vs_ai_baseline"   ],   "voice_targets": [     "Patterns for decentralised organising",     "matched-pair AI version of Oliver Sylvester-Bradley's 2017 essay"   ] } --- Belonging is a superpower – patterns for decentralised organising If you’re in a co‑op, collective, or any non‑hierarchical team with open and inclusive values — and you’re aiming for genuinely horizontal ways of working — this is for you.
It’s a write‑up of a session run by the founders of Loomio, where they shared distilled, repeatable patterns for collaborating well.
You’ve probably heard of Loomio — a simple, effective decision‑making tool that grew out of Enspiral.
The workshop was essentially “the operating system” behind the software.
Rich and Nati delivered the workshop as part of their grand tour, and it’s obvious they’ve been living this for years.
None of the patterns are magical on their own — the value is in how clearly they’re expressed and how deliberately they’re practised.
Take pattern 1: “Intentionally produce counter-culture”.
Many groups already sense this matters, but the phrase that landed was: “belonging is a superpower”.
It’s something teams often claim but don’t design for.
When newcomers can’t find a way in — or long‑timers hoard context, status or access — belonging shrinks.
Unwritten rules start to dominate: who gets invited to the important conversations, whose questions get answered, and who is treated as “credible”.
Pattern 2, “Systematically distribute care labour”, was about making support visible and shared rather than leaving it to the same few people.
Rich described a model where each person is someone’s steward (offering care and attention) and also a stewardee (receiving it).
It’s basic relationship infrastructure, but formalising it makes neglect harder.
Pattern 3 was “Make explicit norms and boundaries”.
Pattern 4 tackled the thing “flat” groups often avoid naming: “Keep talking about power”.
The point isn’t to pretend this doesn’t happen, but to surface it and share it: say who has power in which contexts, rotate roles, step back on purpose, and invite others to step forward.
By then my attention was wobbling — it was past 11am and I’d only had a small cup of tea.
The tag‑team dynamic helped: Nati took over, got everyone stretching, and reset the room’s energy.
Pattern 5, “Make decisions asynchronously”, is so straightforward it’s surprising how often it’s ignored.
It’s also what Loomio was built for.
Pattern 6 named a common headache and turned it into a clear prompt: “Agree how you use tech”.

Rich suggested most team toolsets can be organised into a “holy trinity” for group work: one tool for real‑time communication (chat), one space for asynchronous discussion (email or a forum), and one place for stable reference content (a wiki or document store).
If a group sticks to that agreement, coordination improves and the “where should this go?” noise drops.
Pattern 7 was “Using rhythm to cut information overload”.

The key is matching cadence to purpose: longer rhythms for deeper reflection (for example, quarterly reviews that get people out of routine and reconnect them — creating “peak oxytocin” moments), and shorter cycles for week‑to‑week planning, review and celebration.
Pattern 8 pulled the whole approach together: “Generate new patterns together”.
Loomio’s culture clearly draws on iterative development — build a way of working, test it, learn, adjust, repeat.
Regular review and collective reflection aren’t “nice to have”; they’re a core capability.
Continuous, participatory change can feel slower, but it’s often what keeps a decentralised group coherent over time.
Click for a bigger version For the remainder of the workshop we worked in groups: choose a real challenge, describe a “desired future”, and identify practical next steps.
Our group chose onboarding — specifically, how to help everyone (especially newcomers) gain the “superpower of belonging”.
The “Next steps” section of our worksheet captures what we generated; hopefully some of it is useful in your own context.

semantic_answers.answer: jargon clumps where the writer knows things

answer.why_generic: "Energy" is left undefined — the sentence doesn't specify what actually changed (attention, mood, physical posture), so the metaphor supplies atmosphere rather than concrete meaning.
The infrastructure metaphor gestures at structural support without naming which mechanisms (schedules, check-ins, roles) constitute it beyond what's already stated.

answer.phrase: Better decentralised practice means more capable teams, and more capable teams can deliver more positive change.
answer.what_it_repeats: Restates the same claim twice within a single sentence — 'capable teams' appears as both the effect of the first clause and the cause of the second, without adding new information between the two.

answer.phrase: a well‑structured, thoughtfully designed workshop with timely content
answer.missing_criterion: No criteria given for what made the structure, design, or timing effective — the adjectives assert quality without naming the property judged.

answer.phrase: sharper language for things many groups only sense vaguely
answer.missing_criterion: "Sharper" lacks a comparison basis — sharper than what prior phrasing, and by what measure.
"Stimulating" is asserted without specifying what about the venue produces that effect.

answer.phrase: None of the patterns are magical on their own — the value is in how clearly they’re expressed and how deliberately they’re practised.
answer.missing_context: Reads as a rebuttal to an unstated claim or expectation that the patterns would be presented as magic solutions; that framing isn't otherwise present in the document.

answer.phrase: The point isn’t to pretend this doesn’t happen, but to surface it and share it
answer.missing_context: Defends against an implied objection (that the group ignores or denies power imbalances) that is never actually raised in the text.

answer.why_unnecessary: "Genuinely" performs sincerity/authenticity without specifying what distinguishes genuine from nominal horizontality; the claim could be made directly by naming the practice.
"Real" is used as an authenticity booster rather than specifying what marks belonging as real versus performative.

answer.phrase: Continuous, participatory change can feel slower, but it’s often what keeps a decentralised group coherent over time.
answer.missing_relationship: The 'but' implies a tradeoff mechanism between slowness and coherence, but never states how or why slower participatory change produces coherence.
